blather

BLATH-er · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To blather is to talk long without making sense.

By the third hour of the meeting, the consultant was just blathering, stringing together buzzwords that didn't actually connect to any real plan.

Example

By the end of his rambling toast, the best man was just blathering, and half the guests had stopped listening.

His words had stopped adding up to any clear point -- that loss of real sense, not just length, is what makes it blathering rather than simply a long speech.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

drone on: To drone on is to keep talking in a flat, tedious stream — the listener is bored, but the words still make sense. Blather fails differently: the talk may even sound lively, yet it has stopped adding up to any real meaning at all.

jabber: To jabber is to talk fast and excitedly, the words tumbling out quicker than a listener can follow. Blather has no speed requirement — a person can blather slowly; what marks it is talk that runs long while making no real sense.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

articulate: to express oneself clearly and effectively

Where it sits · how far the speech loses meaning — ramble → blather → gibberish

ramble vs. blather: To ramble is to wander off topic; to blather goes further, suggesting the words barely add up to sense at all.

gibberish vs. blather: Gibberish is the extreme end -- speech that has completely stopped meaning anything, well past blather's merely pointless rambling.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Blather comes from a Scandinavian word for noisy nonsense talk -- its harsh sound was likely chosen to imitate the noisy, meaningless chatter it names.

Use the root in a new word: blether

Use the root in a new word: blether: Blether is a Scottish spelling variant of the very same word, still used informally to mean idle nonsense talk.
